title: Ironic and Humorous Similes
tagline: saying the opposite, with a straight face
why: Ironic similes are everywhere in British and Canadian conversation, and they are easy to misread: as clear as mud means very unclear. Understanding them, and knowing when it's safe to use them, is a mark of real fluency.
know: the ironic frame (about) as + positive adjective + as + something that lacks that quality
eight common ironic and humorous similes, with their British and North American versions
understand: how about and a flat, deadpan voice signal that a simile is ironic
why ironic similes can be funny among friends but risky with strangers or in writing
able: recognise irony instantly and respond to it naturally
use ironic similes to complain, tease or criticise in a light, indirect way
choose a sincere simile instead when irony could be misunderstood
mistakes: The instructions were as clear as mud, so we finished the job in ten minutes.
As clear as mud means very unclear. Read the irony: mud is not clear at all.
The meeting was as boring as watching the paint drying.
About as exciting as watching paint dry. The phrase is fixed; it's also usually ironic (exciting), not boring.
This printer is as useful like a chocolate teapot.
As useful as a chocolate teapot. The frame is as ... as, never as ... like.
We need more paperwork like a fish needs an umbrella.
Like a fish needs a bicycle. The famous version is fixed; changing the noun loses the joke.
(to your manager) Your plan is as sharp as a bowling ball.
Too risky. Use playful insults only about yourself or close friends; at work, say I'm not sure the plan works yet.
bigidea: A sincere simile chooses something that has a lot of the quality: as clear as crystal. An ironic simile does the opposite. It names a positive quality and then compares it to something that completely lacks it: as clear as mud, as useful as a chocolate teapot. The listener's brain notices the clash and gets the joke: the real meaning is the opposite of the adjective.

The little word about is a strong signal: about as useful as, about as exciting as. It sounds like careful understatement, which is exactly what makes it sarcastic. Native speakers deliver these lines deadpan: a flat voice, a straight face, no laugh. The humour comes from pretending to be serious.

Irony is a strong part of British humour and very common in Canada too, but it travels badly. In writing, in a second language, or with people you don't know, it can sound rude or simply be misunderstood. A good rule: be ironic about things, situations and yourself, not about the person in front of you.
hidden: Getting the kids out the door is like herding cats.
Pinning down his position is like nailing jelly to a wall.
Another committee? I need that like I need a hole in the head.
The second half of the game was like watching grass grow.
Affordable apartments downtown are as rare as hen's teeth.
That umbrella is about as much use as a chocolate fireguard.

expressions.example: Thanks for the new expense policy. It's as clear as mud.
expressions.bend: Often drops the first as: clear as mud. Also self-mocking: I hope that wasn't as clear as mud.
expressions.note: The ironic opposite of as clear as crystal or crystal clear. Safe and friendly: it criticises the explanation, not the person.

expressions.e: as useful as a chocolate teapot
expressions.example: This flimsy little umbrella is about as useful as a chocolate teapot.
expressions.bend: About as useful as, about as much use as; British variants include a chocolate fireguard.
expressions.note: Mainly British, but understood in Canada. A teapot made of chocolate would melt as soon as you filled it.

expressions.e: about as much use as a screen door on a submarine

pic.label: a submarine with a screen door

expressions.meaning: completely useless, or making things worse
expressions.example: Without a battery, this smoke detector is about as much use as a screen door on a submarine.
expressions.bend: Also as useful as a screen door on a submarine; sometimes just a screen door on a submarine.
expressions.note: North American: screen doors (with insect mesh) are a summer cottage staple. Stronger than useless: it would actively sink you.

expressions.example: His hint that he wanted the corner office was about as subtle as a sledgehammer.
expressions.bend: Often with about; also subtle as a brick, as subtle as a punch in the face.
expressions.note: Used for hints, advertising, political messages and films. Mildly critical. A neutral alternative: heavy-handed.

expressions.e: as welcome as a skunk at a garden party
expressions.example: The tax inspector was about as welcome as a skunk at a garden party.
expressions.bend: Often as a metaphor: he was the skunk at the garden party (the one who spoiled the fun).
expressions.note: North American; skunks are a familiar summer nuisance in Ontario. Common in political commentary for an unpopular speaker or bad news.

expressions.e: about as exciting as watching paint dry
expressions.example: Honestly, the quarterly report was about as exciting as watching paint dry.
expressions.bend: Also like watching paint dry and like watching grass grow. Fixed: paint dry, not paint drying.
expressions.note: Very common in both British and North American English. Often used about sport, lectures and long meetings.

expressions.e: like a fish needs a bicycle
expressions.example: This town needs another parking garage like a fish needs a bicycle.
expressions.bend: Usually need X like a fish needs a bicycle. Near-synonym: I need that like I need a hole in the head.
expressions.note: Coined by the Australian writer Irina Dunn in 1970 in a feminist slogan about women and men, and made famous by Gloria Steinem. Now used for anything unnecessary.

expressions.e: as sharp as a bowling ball
expressions.meaning: not clever or quick-thinking at all (playful insult)
expressions.example: Before my first coffee, I'm about as sharp as a bowling ball.
expressions.bend: Also as sharp as a marble; compare the understatement not the sharpest tool in the shed.
expressions.note: Use with care: safest about yourself. Calling a colleague this can be hurtful. The sincere opposite is as sharp as a tack (very clever).

culture.how: Chandler's detective Philip Marlowe describes Los Angeles in wild, deadpan similes. Early on, a huge ex-convict in loud clothes is said to stand out on a shabby street about as much as a big spider on a pale cake would. The comic exaggeration became the model for hard-boiled crime writing.
culture.ask: Describe someone or something that really stood out in a place, using a Chandler-style simile.
culture.find: Raymond Chandler Farewell My Lovely similes Moose Malloy

culture.work: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy
culture.how: When an alien fleet arrives over Earth, the narrator says the enormous ships hang in the sky by comparing them to bricks, which famously do not hang anywhere. It's a simile built on a negative: the joke works because you have to undo the comparison to get it.
culture.ask: Can you invent a negative simile of your own, comparing something to what it is not?
culture.find: Douglas Adams Hitchhiker's Guide Vogon ships bricks

culture.how: Love poets of Shakespeare's time compared their ladies' eyes to the sun, lips to coral and skin to snow. In this sonnet the speaker runs through those clichés and admits his lover matches none of them, then says his love is as real as any. It's a parody of tired similes.
culture.ask: Which clichéd compliments or love-song similes would you happily retire today?

culture.how: The title began as a joke. The musician Kathleen Hanna wrote on Kurt Cobain's wall that he smelled like Teen Spirit, a deodorant his girlfriend wore. Cobain didn't know the brand and took it as a rebellious slogan, so a teasing simile became the title of a generation's anthem.
culture.ask: Do you know other famous names or slogans that began as a joke or a misunderstanding?
culture.find: Nirvana Smells Like Teen Spirit title origin Kathleen Hanna

bend.q: A colleague comments quietly on a confusing memo. Which version sounds most natural? ___
opts: Well, that's as clear like mud.
Well, that's clear as a mud.
bend.why: In casual speech the first as is often dropped: clear as mud.

bend.q: Someone adds a deadpan understatement. Which version sounds natural? ___
opts: The new app is about as useful as a chocolate teapot.
The new app is as about useful as a chocolate teapot.
The new app is useful about a chocolate teapot.
bend.why: About goes before the whole frame: about as useful as.

bend.q: A Canadian columnist turns the simile into a metaphor. Which version sounds natural? ___
opts: The finance minister was the skunk at the garden party.
The finance minister was a garden party of skunks.
The finance minister was skunk-like at the garden party.
bend.why: You can drop as welcome as: he was the skunk at the garden party.

bend.q: Someone gives the boring simile a different image. Which version sounds natural? ___
opts: The debate was like watching grass grow.
The debate was like watching grass growing up.
The debate was like watching the grass to grow.
bend.why: Like watching grass grow is a common variant of like watching paint dry.

talk: Shakespeare's Sonnet 130 mocks the clichéd love comparisons of his day. Which similes or compliments do you find tired today, and what would you say instead?
Raymond Chandler's similes are funny because they exaggerate. Describe a terrible hotel room, a boring meeting or an awful meal with two ironic similes.
Role-play: a friend asks for your opinion of a new gadget they bought, which you think is useless. First answer with an ironic simile, then soften it politely.
In your first language, do people use irony in the same way? Is irony safe at work in your culture?
Explain the difference between as sharp as a tack and as sharp as a bowling ball. When would you use the second one, and when never?
